title: Node.js Mastery Test
description: Test your Node.js expertise: libuv, event loop phases, streams, buffer, clustering, async I/O, and Express middlewares.

questions.question: What C library handles asynchronous I/O, thread pool operations, and the Event Loop in Node.js?
options: libuv
V8
OpenSSL
zlib
questions.explanation: Node.js combines Google's V8 JavaScript engine with `libuv`, a multi-platform C library providing asynchronous I/O and thread pool management.

questions.question: What is the order of phases in the Node.js Event Loop?
options: Timers -> Pending Callbacks -> Idle/Prepare -> Poll -> Check -> Close Callbacks
Poll -> Timers -> Check -> Close -> Pending
Microtasks -> Macrotasks -> Timers -> Garbage Collection
Check -> Poll -> Timers -> Pending
questions.explanation: The Node.js event loop cycles through Timers (setTimeout), Pending Callbacks (I/O), Idle/Prepare, Poll (incoming I/O), Check (setImmediate), and Close callbacks.

questions.question: What is the difference between `process.nextTick()` and `setImmediate()` in Node.js?
options: `process.nextTick()` callbacks execute immediately after the current operation finishes before the event loop continues; `setImmediate()` executes in the Check phase
`setImmediate()` executes before `process.nextTick()`
`process.nextTick()` executes after a 10ms delay
They are aliases for the exact same function
questions.explanation: `process.nextTick` queues a callback in the nextTick queue, processed immediately after the active operation before proceeding to the event loop phases.

questions.question: Why are Node.js Streams preferred when processing large multi-gigabyte files?
options: Streams read and process data chunk-by-chunk in small memory buffers without loading the entire file into RAM at once
Streams compress files automatically by 90%
Streams bypass disk I/O completely
Streams only work with JSON formats
questions.explanation: Streaming enables handling data larger than available RAM with minimal memory footprint and faster time-to-first-byte.

questions.question: What is 'Backpressure' in Node.js Streams?
options: A condition where data is being written faster than the destination stream can consume it, signaling the readable stream to pause
A network timeout error in HTTP servers
A CPU bottleneck caused by infinite loops
A memory leak in the garbage collector
questions.explanation: Backpressure occurs when the writable stream's buffer fills up (`write()` returns false), telling the readable stream to pause until 'drain' fires.

questions.question: What is the Node.js `cluster` module used for?
options: Spawning multiple worker processes that share the same server port to take advantage of multi-core CPU architectures
Connecting to distributed database clusters
Clustering CSS files into a single bundle
Synchronizing browser tabs
questions.explanation: Because Node runs on a single main thread, the cluster module forks worker processes running across all available CPU cores.

questions.question: In Express.js, what is the role of the `next()` function inside a middleware?
options: Passes control to the next middleware or route handler in the execution chain
Restarts the Node.js server process
Redirects the client to the next webpage
Sends a 200 OK response immediately
questions.explanation: If a middleware does not end the request-response cycle (e.g. `res.send()`), it must call `next()` to pass control to the subsequent handler.

questions.question: What happens if an unhandled promise rejection occurs in modern Node.js (v15+)?
options: The Node.js process terminates with a non-zero exit code by default
It is silently ignored and the process continues
The server retries the promise indefinitely
The terminal clears and prints a warning
questions.explanation: Since Node 15, unhandled promise rejections default to throwing an UnhandledPromiseRejection exception that crashes the process.

questions.question: What is the primary difference between CommonJS (`require`) and ES Modules (`import`) in Node.js?
options: CommonJS is synchronous and evaluated at runtime; ES Modules are static, asynchronous, and support top-level `await` and tree-shaking
ES Modules only work in the browser
CommonJS is faster than ES Modules in all cases
ES Modules cannot export functions
questions.explanation: ES Modules (ESM) enable static analysis for tree-shaking, asynchronous module loading, and standardized syntax across browser and server.

questions.question: What is the default size of the `libuv` thread pool in Node.js, and how can it be adjusted?
options: Default is 4 threads; adjusted by setting the `UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE` environment variable
Default is 16 threads; adjusted via `package.json`
Default is 1 thread; cannot be changed
Default matches the number of RAM gigabytes
questions.explanation: The libuv thread pool handles disk I/O, DNS lookups, and crypto operations with 4 threads by default, configurable up to 1024.
